items.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
items.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

items.title: Agentic AI for Inclusive Assistive Ecosystems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming assistive technologies, yet many systems remain reactive, fragmented, and insufficiently personalized for individuals with disabilities and neurodivergent conditions. This chapter examines the architectural, design, and governance foundations of trustworthy agentic assistive systems. It synthesizes limitations of conventional approaches, including restricted adaptability, low interoperability, and weak support for user autonomy, and introduces a taxonomy of agentic architectures to guide scalable deployment. The chapter proposes a multi-agent framework integrating multimodal interaction, hybrid reasoning, explainable AI, and health-aware data to enable context-sensitive support. It further addresses privacy, ethical governance, and responsible institutional adoption while outlining future research directions. By bridging architectural innovation with human-centered design, this work advances a forward-looking vision for inclusive intelligent environments.

items.title: Agentic IoT for Urban Renewable Energy
items.abstract: This chapter examines agentic IoT as an emerging paradigm for renewable energy integration in smart cities. Conventional IoT architectures have improved urban energy monitoring and connectivity but remain largely reactive and rule-bound, insufficient for the coordination demands of distributed generation, intermittent supply, electrified mobility, and heterogeneous urban infrastructure. The chapter defines agentic IoT as an urban energy ecosystem in which connected devices, edge nodes, and digital platforms are embedded with situational awareness, dynamic decision-making, multi-agent coordination, adaptive learning, and bounded autonomous execution within predefined safety and policy constraints. A multi-layer conceptual framework is proposed, organized around physical energy assets, IoT sensing and actuation, data and digital twin capabilities, agentic intelligence, platform and ecosystem integration, and governance. The framework positions agentic IoT as an evolution beyond conventional and intelligent IoT toward more autonomous urban energy orchestration.

items.title: AI and Immersive Technologies in Language Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive technologies are expanding opportunities for language learners to obtain feedback, revise writing, and rehearse communication. Their educational value depends on how these opportunities support learning and informed participation. Wu et al. (2025) locate recent technological developments within broader concerns about learner affect, teacher development, and immersive learning. This wider perspective is useful for understanding the nine articles in this special issue. Together, they examine how technological assistance interacts with critical thinking, authorship, communicative practice, and teacher agency. We bring these contributions into dialogue to consider the pedagogical conditions under which innovation supports learners’ developing capabilities.

items.title: AI and Machine Learning Approaches to Address Cybersecurity Challenges in Smart Grid Systems
items.abstract: Smart grid systems have been utilized with artificial intelligence (AI) which has substantially improved their efficiency and reliability. Nevertheless, with the development of smart grids into more intricate, networked, and data-intensive systems, a smart grid is becoming more susceptible to cybercrime. The chapter handles the problem of cybersecurity available within smart grid systems shedding light on the especial vulnerabilities that lies in the fact that they are digital and automated. It talks about the application of AI-based solutions to deal with such risks and it focuses on approaches that include anomaly detection, real-time threat responsiveness, and forecast risk. Besides, the chapter is also about AI aimed at protecting the communication network and providing more effective identification processes, and autonomic safe work. Through interpretation of case studies and projections in the real world, this paper gives a holistic idea of how AI can enhance the cybersecurity infrastructure in smart grid infrastructures.

items.title: AI and the double competence gap in dental education: towards symbiotic intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the knowledge infrastructure of healthcare. From diagnostic support and image interpretation to patient communication and clinical decision-making, AI-supported technologies, including generative AI, are changing the conditions under which healthcare professionals work. Dentistry is no exception. Recent research highlights emerging applications of AI in dental practice, while international reviews suggest growing opportunities and challenges associated with integrating AI into dental education. However, the rapid development of AI-supported technologies raises questions about how effectively professional education and continuing professional development can respond to evolving competency requirements. This raises a central question: How can dental education and continuing professional development respond to the potential double competence gap associated with AI-enabled dental practice?In this Opinion article, we address this question by proposing a conceptual framework that distinguishes between an initial education-practice gap and a continuing professional competence gap. Drawing on the concepts of AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence, and symbiotic intelligence, we discuss how dental education may develop and assess the competencies required for critical, ethical, and responsible AI use while preserving independent clinical reasoning, professional accountability, and patient-centred care.The rapid development of artificial intelligence raises important questions about how dental education can maintain the relevance of its curricula while safeguarding established standards of clinical competence, patient safety, and professional accountability. Although international reviews indicate growing interest in AI applications within dental education, systematic curricular integration appears to vary across institutions and educational contexts (9,10,24). Such variation should not necessarily be interpreted as resistance to technological change, as cautious implementation may also reflect legitimate concerns about educational quality, clinical validity, ethical safeguards, and the availability of robust evidence. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education raise questions about whether current educational provision adequately addresses emerging AIrelated competency requirements, potentially contributing to the two dimensions of the proposed double competence gap. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education suggest that this may contribute to reinforcing an already existing double competence gap When generative artificial intelligence became widely accessible through platform-based services such as ChatGPT in the autumn of 2022, many assumed that it would primarily affect the technology sector. However, when we tested a professional version of ChatGPT (GPT-4) in medicine, and partly in dental and psychology education, in March 2023, it was already apparent that this represented a technological paradigm shift with potentially farreaching implications across professional education programmes (1,2).While AI capabilities have developed rapidly in recent years in the health sciences (3)(4)(5)(6)(7)(8)(9)(10)(11), their integration into dental education presents a different set of challenges. Curriculum development, faculty preparation, assessment design, and clinical governance require careful consideration and cannot necessarily follow the pace of technological innovation. Recent reviews indicate that AI-related educational initiatives are emerging, but their integration into formal curricula and assessment practices remains variable. Several key explanations emerge from the literature: already overcrowded curricula, insufficient profession-specific digital competence among educators, and a lack of structured implementation (9,10,24). This potential misalignment between technological developments and structured educational provision provides an important rationale for examining the proposed double competence gap.Dental education has previously incorporated technologies such as digital radiography, simulation, intraoral scanning, and computer-aided design and manufacturing (29). These developments offer relevant lessons for AI integration: new technologies require faculty development, opportunities for supervised practice, alignment with clinical tasks, and assessment of what students can actually do. However, the current AI transition differs in its breadth and pace. Generative AI can be used across clinical reasoning, communication, learning, and assessment, including through tools that students access independently of their institutions. Moreover, the capabilities and limitations of these systems may change within a single curriculum cycle. Dental programmes should therefore draw on established approaches to curricular implementation while developing a more continuous process for reviewing AIrelated learning outcomes, teaching cases, and assessment practices.The Norwegian national curriculum regulations for healthcare professional education (RETHOS) emphasise that educational programmes should respond to society's current and future competence needs. However, AI is not explicitly addressed in the national curriculum regulations for dentistry, medicine, or psychology (12)(13)(14). Similarly, the Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT)'s national evaluation of medical education in 2025 provides limited explicit discussion of AI (15). These observations should be interpreted with caution. The absence of explicit AI terminology in national regulations or evaluation reports does not necessarily imply that AIrelated competencies are absent from institutional curricula, teaching practices, or assessment arrangements. National frameworks may deliberately emphasise enduring, technology-neutral professional competencies, allowing educational institutions to adapt their programmes to technological developments without requiring frequent regulatory revisions.Nevertheless, the limited explicit attention to AI in these national documents raises relevant questions about how emerging AI-related competencies are interpreted, operationalised, and assessed within individual educational programmes. International reviews have identified variation in the integration of AI into dental education, including challenges related to curriculum development, faculty preparedness, and the assessment of AI-related competencies (9,10,24).From the perspective of the proposed double competence gap framework, the central concern is therefore not simply whether AI is explicitly mentioned in national policy documents, but whether educational programmes systematically develop and assess the competencies required for responsible AI use in dental practice. Addressing this question requires empirical examination of institutional curricula, learning outcomes, educational activities, and assessment practices rather than relying solely on national policy analysis.Although the policy examples discussed here are drawn from Norway, the distinction between national competency frameworks, institutional curricula, and actual educational practices may also be relevant internationally. However, the extent to which the proposed double competence gap applies across different countries and dental education systems requires context-specific empirical investigation.The increasing integration of AI into healthcare knowledge infrastructures may also have epistemological implications for professional education. As AI systems become involved in information retrieval, diagnostic support, and clinical decision-making, questions arise concerning how professional knowledge is produced, evaluated, interpreted, and applied. These developments may gradually reshape aspects of professional roles and clinical reasoning, although their scope, pace, and educational consequences remain uncertain. Rather than predicting a specific timeline for such changes, dental education should develop adaptable approaches that enable students and practising professionals to critically evaluate emerging technologies while maintaining established standards of clinical expertise and professional accountability (16,18). Professional digital competence and AI literacy should become integral components of both the knowledge infrastructure and professional competence, and conceptual frameworks need to be developed that account for professionspecific AI use across both urban and rural patient contexts (17).At the same time, the challenge extends far beyond today's dentist education. The vast majority of today's practising professionals completed their education long before generative artificial intelligence became part of professional practice. Consequently, they have not necessarily received systematic training in how such AI systems can be used professionally, what their limitations are, or which ethical and legal challenges they may entail.We propose the concept of a double competence gap to describe two distinct but interconnected potential mismatches between the competencies required for responsible professional practice in increasingly AI-enabled dental healthcare and the competencies systematically developed through initial dental education and continuing professional development. A competence gap is understood here as a discrepancy between demonstrable professional capabilities and the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to perform relevant professional tasks safely, effectively, and ethically. Importantly, such gaps cannot be inferred solely from the availability of new technologies or the absence of explicit AI terminology in educational policy documents; their existence and extent require empirical investigation.The first competence gap, which we term the initial education-practice gap, concerns the potential misalignment between undergraduate dental education and the evolving competencies required in AI-enabled dental practice. International reviews suggest that the systematic integration of AI-related learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment practices in dental education remains uneven (9,10,24). This raises questions about whether existing educational provision adequately prepares students for the critical and clinically appropriate use of AI in future dental practice. Although students may independently engage with generative AI and other AI-supported technologies, such engagement does not necessarily constitute systematic development of profession-specific AI literacy. The central educational concern is therefore whether curricula, learning outcomes, teaching practices, and assessment arrangements adequately prepare students to critically evaluate AI-generated information, recognise its limitations, and integrate appropriate AI-supported decisionmaking with established clinical knowledge and professional judgement.The second competence gap, termed the continuing professional competence gap, concerns practising dentists whose initial professional education preceded the widespread availability of contemporary generative AI and other emerging AI applications. These professionals may encounter new technological expectations without having had equivalent opportunities for structured education in AI evaluation, clinical applicability, patient safety, data protection, and professional accountability. However, the extent of this gap is likely to vary across practitioners, clinical settings, previous digital experience, and access to continuing professional development.The conceptual contribution of the double competence gap framework lies in connecting these two educational challenges across the professional life course. Whereas AI literacy describes a set of relevant competencies, and Professional Digital Competence provides a broader perspective on technology-related professional capabilities, the double competence gap framework draws attention to the potential misalignment between competency requirements and educational provision at two different stages of professional development. It thereby offers a basis for examining how initial education, curriculum and assessment, faculty development, and continuing professional development can respond to changing professional requirements.We present the double competence gap as a conceptual and empirically testable proposition rather than as an established finding across dental education. Its educational significance depends on whether these proposed mismatches can be identified, assessed, and addressed in specific institutional and professional contexts.Empirically investigating the proposed double competence gap requires distinguishing between shortcomings in educational provision and demonstrable deficiencies in professional competence. The initial education -practice gap could be examined through curriculum mapping, IADT-guidelines (34IADT, 2026), analysis of intended learning outcomes and assessment practices, interviews with educators and students, and performance-based assessments of AI-related clinical competencies. The continuing professional competence gap could be investigated through research informed knowledge (33e.g. Ji et al., 2025), surveys, interviews, and scenario-based assessments involving practising dentists with different levels of professional experience and AI exposure. Importantly, the absence of explicit AI-related learning outcomes or structured training would indicate a potential gap in educational provision, but would not, in itself, demonstrate insufficient professional competence. Establishing a competence gap would require comparing observable performance with independently defined, clinically relevant competency standards, while accounting for differences in professional roles, practice contexts, and access to continuing professional development.Addressing the proposed double competence gap requires conceptual clarity regarding AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence (PDC), and symbiotic intelligence (SI). Although these concepts are closely related, they represent distinct dimensions of professional competence and human -AI interaction in dental education and practice.AI literacy refers to the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to understand, evaluate, and appropriately use AI systems within specific professional contexts. items.title: AI CHAT ASSISTANT FOR ONLINE BUSINESS
items.abstract: Online businesses must answer product questions, explain policies, guide purchases and resolve order-related concerns across multiplechannels. Human-only support can be costly and slow during peak demand, while rigid rule-based chatbots struggle with varied wording andmulti-step questions. This paper presents a conceptual design for an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chat Assistant for Online Business thatcombines natural language understanding, retrieval from approved business knowledge, controlled access to commerce services andescalation to human staff. The proposed assistant interprets customer intent, retrieves relevant product and policy information, generatesgrounded responses, and invokes permitted actions such as checking order status only after appropriate authentication. The architectureemphasizes factual consistency, privacy, security, accessibility and measurable service quality. It also describes a developmentmethodology, evaluation metrics, risk controls and a staged deployment plan. Since this is a design-oriented study, no original performanceresults are claimed; the proposed evaluation must be conducted using representative customer queries and verified business data.

items.title: AI Chatbot-Assisted Teaching and Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The instructional effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue tools in higher education varies across contexts and depends on multiple moderation mechanisms. This structured evidence synthesis of eight studies identifies four moderation dimensions: task embedding depth, feedback granularity, teacher orchestration intensity, and discipline verification pressure. These dimensions are examined through task cycles, feedback characteristics, teacher intervention, and verification requirements. The findings show that higher intensity configurations with structured task embedding, layered feedback, teacher orchestration, and content verification are associated with higher composite coding indices across learning gains, engagement, trust, and knowledge transfer. A four-stage closed-loop learning pathway is proposed to support the pedagogical integration of AI dialogue tools. The findings highlight the importance of moderation mechanisms, teacher orchestration, and feedback granularity in designing effective AI-supported learning environments.

items.abstract: For this study, we first did an assessment of students’ motivation for HE and their academic experience so far; we then examined university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their formal learning. The participants were students enrolled into different courses at Cosmopolitan university, Abuja. This research survey examines university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their higher education learning. A descriptive survey research method was used. Specifically, a questionnaire was used to collect data. The participants were students enrolled in different courses at Cosmopolitan university in Abuja, Nigeria. The results showed that the participants had positive perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning in affective, cognitive, and cognitive domains. Students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning did not differ significantly according to perceived digital dependency. However, students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning were influenced by their use of some AI tools and perceived digital competency. items.title: AI Universal Design for Learning and Inclusive Teaching Practices
items.abstract: This chapter explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), universal design for learning (UDL), and inclusive teaching practices in higher education to enhance institutional performance. It examines how AI supports personalised learning, accessibility, and differentiated instruction aligned with UDL principles. Using conceptual analysis, the chapter shows that inclusive teaching improves engagement, retention, and equitable outcomes. It also situates inclusive pedagogy within social justice frameworks. Findings indicate that AI strengthens flexibility and responsiveness, while UDL promotes proactive accessibility for diverse learners. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and unequal access remain critical considerations.

items.title: AI-Assisted 8-Bit Processor Design Using Digital Logic Components for Educational Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing complexity of modern processors presents challenges for students in understanding the fundamental principles of computer architecture and digital logic design. Traditional microprocessors and microcontrollers often conceal their internal operations, making it difficult for learners to visualize how individual logic components work together to execute instructions.This study aims to develop an educational processor model that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistance with digital logic design to improve the understanding of processor architecture and instruction execution. The proposed system will utilize fundamental digital logic components, including logic gates, registers, an Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), a control unit, a program counter, and memory, to demonstrate the basic operations of an 8-bit processor. AI assistance will be explored to support circuit design, logic analysis, instruction decoding, and troubleshooting during the development process. The processor will demonstrate the fetch–decode–execute cycle and basic arithmetic, logical, and data transfer operations through a practical and observable implementation. Functional testing and simulation will be used to verify the correctness of the processor's operations and the reliability of its component interconnections. By combining AI-assisted development with hands-on digital logic implementation, the study aims to provide a practical, accessible, and cost-effective educational resource for students studying computer engineering, digital electronics, and computer architecture. The proposed system is expected to bridge the gap between theoretical concepts and practical hardware implementation while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and independent learning. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, 8-Bit Processor, Digital Logic Components, Computer Architecture, Educational Applications, Instruction Execution

items.title: AI-Based Decision Support for Asset Allocation Management as a Component of Business Models under Market Uncertainty
items.abstract: Objectives The aim of the study was to identify and evaluate the possibilities of using artificial intelligence assistants to support decision-making processes related to asset allocation, treated as an important component of the business model of an enterprise operating under conditions of market uncertainty. Material and methods The study was conducted on the example of three companies from the construction sector listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange: Budimex S.A., Polimex Mostostal S.A., and Mirbud S.A. The analysis covered the years 2020–2024 and was based on two groups of data: annual fundamental indicators and daily closing stock prices. In the fundamental part, return on equity, debt ratio, asset utilization ratio, and the Altman discriminant model were used to construct a synthetic fundamental index. In the market part, daily logarithmic rates of return and the Sharpe ratio were calculated. Results The results indicate that AI assistants can effectively support the analytical process by accelerating calculations and increasing the repeatability of the procedure. At the same time, differences in model performance were observed, indicating the risk of errors in data interpretation. Conclusions The study demonstrates that AI can be a useful tool supporting asset allocation management; however, its effectiveness depends on data quality, the precision of the analytical procedure, and human supervision. The findings highlight the importance of control mechanisms and model triangulation in AI-supported decision-making processes.

items.title: AI-based personalized learning and academic performance in computing and engineering higher education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for personalized learning in higher education has generated growing interest in their effects on student outcomes, yet comparative evidence remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether AI-based personalized learning is associated with differences in objectively measured academic performance, compared with instruction without the AI component, among higher education students. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in April 2026. Eligible studies implemented an AI system that adapted content, feedback, pacing or recommendations to learners, included a concurrent or historical comparator group, and reported an objective academic-performance outcome. Of 84 unique records, four controlled studies (420 students), all conducted in computing and engineering courses, met the criteria: one cluster-randomized study, one study reporting random allocation without procedural detail, one non-randomized study with a concurrent control, and one study with a historical control. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 or ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results A random-effects model (REML) yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 1.01 (95% CI 0.33–1.68); with the Hartung-Knapp small-sample adjustment the interval widened to −0.10–2.11 and included no effect. Heterogeneity was substantial ( I 2 = 89%; τ 2 = 0.41), and the 95% prediction interval (−0.42–2.43) also included no effect. Leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.80 to 1.22. Two studies were at serious risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was very low. Discussion The available controlled studies suggest a potentially beneficial association between AI-based personalized learning and academic performance in computing and engineering courses, but the magnitude and consistency of this association remain uncertain, and causal conclusions are not warranted. items.title: AI-Based Skin Disease Prediction System Using ConvNeXt-Tiny with Explainable Visualization and Phase Guidance
items.abstract: Skin diseases are common, but seeing a dermatologist is not easy for everyone, especially in under-served regions. Many deep-learning classifiers are heavy, hard to interpret and stop at a class label. We present MediCare AI, a lightweight screening system that sorts skin images into seven disease categories by fully fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with AdamW, cosine learning-rate decay, label smoothing and early stopping. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping shows which parts of the image drove each prediction. A Streamlit app accepts uploaded photos and live camera frames, reports the confidence and a rough three-level visible phase, and gives treatment suggestions and preventive advice through a generative service, with a local offline fallback. A single network reached roughly 80%–90% validation accuracy. The tool is meant for education and early screening, not as a replacement for professional diagnosis. Index Terms—skin disease classification, ConvNeXt, transfer learning, Grad-CAM, explainable artificial intelligence, Streamlit.

items.title: AI-Based Verification of Tyre Wear and Tear Using MobileNet-Based Image Classification
items.abstract: This research manuscript presents a proposed artificial intelligence-based approach for verifying tyre wear and tear using image classification and a MobileNet-based deep learning model. The objective is to explore how computer vision can support the identification of tyre wear conditions and assist vehicle maintenance and road-safety practices.The proposed workflow includes collecting tyre images, preparing and preprocessing the image dataset, training a MobileNet-based classification model, and evaluating its performance using appropriate classification metrics. The approach is intended to provide a foundation for a practical tyre inspection support system.The manuscript discusses the background, proposed methodology, potential applications, evaluation plan, limitations, and future scope of AI-based tyre wear detection. Reliable evaluation requires access to the original dataset, trained model, and test results. Since verified experimental results are not currently available, this manuscript does not claim a measured accuracy or experimentally validated performance.The work is relevant to automotive engineering, computer vision, deep learning, vehicle maintenance, and intelligent inspection systems.

items.title: AI-Based Virtual Screening of NLRP3 Inflammasome-Targeting Drug Candidates for Alzheimer’s Disease and Evaluation of Blood–Brain Barrier Permeability
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly. Traditional drugs targeting Aβ and Tau proteins face development bottlenecks. In recent years, studies have shown that NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated neuroinflammation in the brain is a key mechanism in the pathogenesis of AD. However, the number of existing NLRP3-specific inhibitors is limited, and they generally suffer from insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration. This study aims to combine artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning technologies to construct a multi-task screening model that can simultaneously predict the inhibitory activity of small molecule NLRP3 and its ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier, providing an efficient and low-cost computational screening technology solution for the development of novel anti-inflammatory drugs for Alzheimer's disease. It uses AlphaFold to obtain target protein structures and combines them with the ZINC20/PubChem chemical database to construct a compound dataset. Using Python as the core tool, a random forest multi-task machine learning model was built using the Google Colab cloud platform. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, lipid solubility (LogP), and polar surface area (TPSA) were selected as input features for the model. The drug’s NLRP3 activity and BBB penetration were used as the core prediction labels for model training and cross-validation. The model demonstrated high predictive performance in 5-fold cross-validation, with an average accuracy of 68.89% for predicting NLRP3 activity and an average accuracy of 97.78% for predicting blood-brain barrier penetration. Feature importance analysis confirmed that LogP and TPSA are the most critical physicochemical features that determine whether candidate molecules can penetrate the blood-brain barrier. Several candidate small molecules with both NLRP3 inhibition potential and BBB penetration were screened from a large-scale candidate molecule library. This study successfully constructed a low-cost, easy-to-implement AI-assisted drug screening system for neurological diseases, which can provide data support for the development of lead compounds for novel anti-inflammatory targeted drugs for Alzheimer's disease.

items.abstract: This chapter presents an artificial intelligence-driven battery health monitoring framework for sustainable electric vehicle applications. The chapter also explores intelligent battery management, fault diagnosis, digital twins, smart grids, Internet of Things, and Vehicle-to-Grid integration for future energy systems.

items.title: AI-Driven Data Automation and Financial Reporting Timeliness and Accuracy: Evidence from Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Late and error-prone government accounts weaken legislative oversight and citizen scrutiny. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven data automation is associated with the timeliness and accuracy of financial reports in Nigeria's federal public sector. Using a ten-year balanced panel (2015–2024) of five purposively selected institutions, the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement, the study scores documentary evidence from annual reports, financial statements and official AI-implementation documents on a five-point (0–4) rubric and estimates pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged panel regressions, interpreted through agency theory. AI-driven data automation is positively and significantly associated with the composite measure of reporting timeliness and accuracy (pooled β = 0.717, R² = 0.845; within-institution β = 0.706, within R² = 0.818). The association remains positive and significant after controlling for a common time trend (β = 0.641), in first differences (β = 0.761) and when automation is lagged one year (β = 0.631). A one-point higher automation score is therefore associated with roughly 0.6 to 0.8 points higher reporting quality on the five-point scale. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. The findings support targeted investment in AI-enabled data capture, validation and reconciliation, accompanied by governance arrangements, human review and skills development.

items.title: AI-Driven Mindfulness-Based Mental Health Support for Mothers of Children With Autism
items.abstract: Mothers caring for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder often face ongoing stress, emotional challenges, and significant caregiving responsibilities. These factors can affect family dynamics and the quality of support services available for disabilities. Although traditional counselling can offer some psychological relief, it may lack personalization, scalability, or ongoing monitoring. This chapter presents a mindfulness-based intervention enhanced by artificial intelligence, utilizing established techniques like Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction to provide flexible and accessible mental health resources. By combining AI with structured mindfulness practices, this approach seeks to improve emotional regulation, promote increased caregiver engagement, and foster better collaboration with disability service organizations. The chapter emphasizes that AI-enhanced mindfulness can serve as a valuable resource to bolster caregiver resilience and facilitate more efficient and responsive delivery of disability services.

items.title: AI-Driven Multimodal Intelligence in Quantum AI, BCI, and Roadmap to Next-Generation Intelligent Systems
items.abstract: The transition of artificial intelligence from unimodal learning systems to integrated multimedia and multimodal intelligence marks a critical shift in how machines perceive, reason, and interact with complex environments. Despite recent advances, current architectures remain constrained by computational scalability, limited contextual awareness, and indirect human–machine communication. This chapter explores future trajectories in AI-driven multimodal intelligence through the convergence of quantum artificial intelligence (QAI), brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), and next-generation deployment frameworks. The chapter adopts a conceptual research approach to examine how quantum-enhanced learning mechanisms can accelerate multimodal data fusion, optimize high-dimensional representations, and enable real-time cognitive analytics. In parallel, emerging BCI technologies are analyzed as transformative interfaces that integrate neural signals into intelligent systems, fostering adaptive environments responsive to human cognitive and emotional states. Together, these innovations signal a paradigm shift from algorithm-centric automation towards collaborative human–AI ecosystems. A phased roadmap is proposed, outlining foundational integration, cognitive expansion, and long-term human–machine symbiosis. Particular attention is given to developing economies, especially African contexts, where infrastructural constraints coexist with significant opportunities for leapfrogging through AI-enabled healthcare, education, logistics, and governance systems. Ethical governance, digital inclusion, workforce development, and data sovereignty are critically discussed as foundational pillars for sustainable deployment. The chapter concludes that responsible convergence across quantum computing, neurotechnology, and multimodal architectures supported by interdisciplinary collaboration and inclusive policy frameworks is essential for translating experimental innovations into scalable societal impact, positioning AI as a catalyst for equitable global development.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN PRECISION ONCOLOGY: REVOLUTIONIZING PERSONALIZED CANCER THERAPY
items.abstract: Precision oncology is an approach in which cancer treatment is selected according to the molecular, genomic and clinical characteristics of an individual patient and tumour. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing, can analyses large and complex datasets generated by genomics, pathology, radiology and electronic health records. AI may help identify actionable biomarkers, predict treatment response and resistance, support drug discovery, match patients to clinical trials and anticipate adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This review describes the principles of AI-driven precision oncology, major biomarkers, pharmacogenomics, mechanisms of selected targeted and immune therapies, drug-specific adverse effects, AI-assisted toxicity prediction, clinical workflow, advantages, limitations, ethical considerations and future directions. Selected therapies including osimertinib, trastuzumab, dabrafenib/trametinib, olaparib and pembrolizumab demonstrate how molecular findings can be translated into individualized treatment. The future of oncology is likely to involve multimodal AI combined with longitudinal molecular monitoring and multidisciplinary clinical decision-making.

items.title: AI-Enabled Animal Behavior Analysis for Translational Pharmacology and Therapeutic Discovery
items.abstract: Animal behavior is a critical endpoint in preclinical pharmacology, toxicology, and therapeutic discovery, yet conventional behavioral scoring remains labor-intensive, low-dimensional, and difficult to reproduce across laboratories. Artificial intelligence (AI) can now quantify behavior from video with greater spatial, temporal, and phenotypic resolution. This review summarizes how object detection, markerless pose estimation, unsupervised behavioral segmentation, foundation models, and autonomous analysis agents are reshaping behavioral phenotyping. General-purpose object detectors rapidly localize and track animals, whereas open-source pose-estimation tools extend measurement beyond centroid tracking to body-part trajectories and fine motor patterns; paired with supervised classifiers, they have matched human scoring and exceeded some commercial systems. Technical accuracy alone does not establish behavioral construct validity or pharmacological validity. Unsupervised methods such as Motion Sequencing represent drug responses and disease-model phenotypes as structured changes in behavioral states rather than only as predefined endpoints, providing high-dimensional fingerprints of pharmacological action. Segmentation and tracking foundation models may reduce annotation burden but require validation across species, strain, sex, apparatus, and paradigm. AI agents may assist with literature review, code generation, analysis auditing, and figure production but must remain within transparent, human-supervised workflows. In behavioral pharmacology, pose estimation is established as a measurement method and emerging as a drug-effect endpoint, supervised classification and unsupervised segmentation are emerging, and foundation models and agents remain prospective. AI-enabled behavioral analysis can become a reproducible phenotyping layer for drug discovery and toxicology if researchers adopt open pipelines, rigorous validation, and reporting standards, rather than replacing one opaque measurement system with another.

items.title: AI-Enabled Compliance Monitoring and Adherence to Financial Regulations in Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Compliance with financial regulations is central to public accountability, yet monitoring adherence across ministries, departments and agencies is difficult at the scale and complexity of Nigeria's federal public sector. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled compliance monitoring is associated with adherence to financial regulations in Nigeria's federal public sector. A balanced panel of five federal institutions, the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement is observed over 2015–2024. Documentary evidence from annual reports, audit-related documents and AI-implementation documents is scored on a five-point (0–4) rubric and analysed with pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. AI-enabled compliance monitoring is positively and significantly associated with regulatory compliance (pooled β = 0.719, R² = 0.923; fixed-effects β = 0.742, within R² = 0.858). The association remains positive and significant after controlling for a common time trend (β = 0.629), in first differences (β = 0.554) and when monitoring is lagged one year (β = 0.657). A conservative reading is that one additional point of monitoring adoption is associated with roughly 0.55 to 0.65 points higher regulatory compliance. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. The findings support investment in AI-enabled monitoring as one component of a functioning compliance chain, accompanied by data quality, regulatory clarity, staff capacity, governance arrangements and human review.

items.title: AI-Enabled Patient Profiling for Personalized Nursing Care and Health Support: Scoping Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AI-enabled patient profiling has been proposed to organize heterogeneous patient data and support personalized nursing care and health support. Given the growing use of AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), digital phenotyping, and digital twins in health care, it is important to clarify how patient profiling has been conceptualized, applied, and evaluated in nursing-relevant contexts. OBJECTIVE This scoping review aimed to examine and report the available evidence on AI-enabled patient profiling for personalized nursing care and health support. METHODS This scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to May 18, 2026, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase. Eligible studies used AI or computational intelligence methods to construct, classify, apply, validate, or evaluate patient profiles or related patient representations relevant to personalized nursing care or health support. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed full texts, and charted data using a predefined form. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively using an input-process-output framework. RESULTS A total of 61 studies were included. AI-enabled patient profiling was represented through patient profiles, patient or user personas, digital phenotypes, patient segments, clinical subtypes, digital twins, and LLM-enabled personalization. Included studies used diverse data sources, including electronic health records, nursing records, patient-reported outcomes, questionnaires, mobile app data, wearable and sensor data, engagement logs, and textual or conversational data. Common AI approaches included machine learning, clustering, deep learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, digital twin modeling, and LLMs. Applications focused on personalized education, self-management support, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, remote monitoring, decision support, follow-up care, and shared decision-making. Most studies evaluated algorithmic performance, feasibility, usability, or system development, whereas fewer studies examined profile validity, actionability, equity, workflow integration, or long-term nursing-sensitive and patient-centered outcomes. CONCLUSIONS Existing evidence positions AI-enabled patient profiling as an emerging data-to-action mechanism for personalized nursing care and health support rather than as a mature clinical intervention. Future research should strengthen conceptual clarity, validate the profile, establish explicit pathways linking profiles to actions, incorporate nurse and patient involvement, assess equity and safety, and evaluate implementation in real-world nursing settings. items.title: AI-Enhanced Assignment Grading in Higher Education
items.abstract: The digitalization of education is critical for educational modernization and equitable access to quality education. However, higher education institutions face significant challenges in homework grading due to large student enrollments, including low grading efficiency and insufficient personalized feedback. This paper presents a general multi-agent framework leveraging large language models for automated assignment grading in higher education. The framework employed seven specialized agents: document reader, format converter, parser, artificial intelligence grading, data aggregation, report generation, and error handling. This domain-agnostic framework can be adapted to various disciplines by configuring appropriate grading criteria. A case study across nine classes with 258 students demonstrated 14–39 times efficiency improvement, reducing single-class processing time from 32–63 minutes to 1.6–2.3 minutes. The results indicated that the approach significantly reduced teachers' workload while providing targeted feedback, advancing digital transformation in education.

items.title: AI-Powered Predictive Analytics and Its Relationship with Budgeting Efficiency and Financial Accountability in Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Budgets are the plans against which public financial reports are judged, and weak forecasting undermines both budget credibility and accountability. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered predictive analytics is associated with budgeting efficiency and financial accountability in Nigeria's federal public sector. A balanced panel of five federal institutions, the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement, is observed over 2015–2024. Documentary evidence from annual reports, audit-related documents and AI-implementation documents is scored on a five-point (0–4) rubric and analysed with pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. Predictive analytics adoption is positively and significantly associated with budgeting efficiency and accountability (pooled β = 0.694, R² = 0.853; fixed-effects β = 0.712, within R² = 0.845). The association remains significant after adjusting for a common trend (β = 0.639), in first differences (β = 0.727) and with a one-year lag (β = 0.585). The lagged estimate is the smallest of the specifications, consistent with, though not proof of, a maturation period during which models learn from data and users learn to rely on forecasts. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. The results support investment in forecasting capability and data infrastructure, with realistic expectations about time-to-benefit, accompanied by data-quality programmes, staff training, publication of forecast errors and expert review of model outputs.

This chapter investigates predictive pipelines, benchmarking models (SVM) and random forests, (CNN and LSTM) and validation, ethics, privacy, and adaptive intervention frameworks in an attempt to encourage equitable, transparent, and scalable learning intervention systems.

items.title: AI-Supported Inclusive Teaching, Learning, and Assessment Practices
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming educational systems, offering innovative pathways for enhancing inclusive teaching, learning and assessment practices. In the context of disability support, AI-driven tools provide opportunities to personalize instruction, improve accessibility and strengthen institutional performance through data-informed decision-making. However, despite these potentials, some educational institutions face challenges in effectively integrating AI into inclusive education practices. This chapter therefore examines how AI-supported instructional strategies, adaptive learning systems and intelligent assessment tools can address diverse learner needs. It critically analyzes ethical concerns, implementation barriers and capacity gaps associated with AI adoption in education. The chapter proposes a conceptual framework linking AI integration, inclusive pedagogy and institutional outcomes. It further provides actionable suggestions for stakeholders seeking to leverage AI for sustainable disability support and improved institutional effectiveness.

items.title: AI‐Guided Intrinsic and Extrinsic Photocorrosion Inhibition of III–V Semiconductors for Durable Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting
items.abstract: Group III–V semiconductors are suitable for solar‐driven hydrogen production due to precise lattice matching (for tandem device combinations), high carrier mobilities (>10 3 cm 2 V –1 s –1 ), tunable bandgaps (1.1–2.5 eV), strong absorption coefficients (>10 5 cm –1 ), and a large range of doping possibilities. GaInP 2 , GaAs, and InP have a theoretical solar‐to‐hydrogen efficiency of more than 20%. Still, their high susceptibility to chemical and photochemical corrosion during prolonged photoelectrochemical water splitting (PEC‐WS) is a major industrial hurdle. This review comprehensively covers critical strategies to enhance the photostability of group III–V semiconductors for industrial‐scale PEC‐WS, emphasizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) support. We discuss three main intrinsic and extrinsic strategies that include (i) AI‐driven crystal structure modification and faceted growth control, (ii) physical and chemical surface passivation coupled with machine learning for passivation material screening strategies, and (iii) combining III–V semiconductors with appropriate band‐aligned materials via preferable heterojunctions, utilizing algorithms to select optimal compositions. We examine the underlying mechanisms of each strategy and conclude with perspectives on achieving optimal materials for PEC‐WS using advanced AI and ML screening tools. Implementing these effective modification strategies, the wide commercial potential of III–V photoelectrodes for PEC‐WS technology can be unlocked.

items.title: Algorithmic HRM and freelancer capabilities in Sri Lanka: constraints and the role of social support
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how algorithmic human resource management (HRM) constrains the capabilities of platform-based freelancers in Sri Lanka, and how informal social support helps them sustain these capabilities. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative design, the research draws on 41 in-depth interviews and applies reflexive thematic analysis, informed by the capability approach and social support theory. Findings Four interconnected themes were identified: algorithmic work allocation constrains income security and temporal autonomy, digital enforcement and dispute processes undermine procedural fairness and recognition, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven market changes constrain capabilities through skill devaluation, and informal social support functions as an extra-platform capability infrastructure. Practical implications The findings point to implications for platform design, regulatory policy and emerging forms of worker organising, particularly in contexts marked by weak institutional protections. Originality/value This study draws on the capability approach and social support theory to make two contributions. First, it identifies a cumulative, reputation-based pathway through which algorithmic HRM constrains capabilities in knowledge-intensive freelancing. This extends current understanding beyond the transaction-based gig work that has dominated prior research. Second, it shows that informal social support contributes directly to capability development but cannot alter the structural algorithmic mechanisms that govern visibility, income security and procedural voice.

items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints. This survey examines MLLM alignment through two complementary gaps: the Modality Gap, concerning cross-modal correspondence and the use of task-relevant evidence, and the Intent Gap, concerning behavior relative to specified goals, constraints, and human expectations. We organize the literature along six dimensions: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. Across these dimensions, we link alignment mechanisms and supervision assumptions to the failures they target and the evidence supporting their effectiveness. Our analysis clarifies what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment, together with the limitations of their underlying supervision. We further summarize evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels, emphasizing evidence dependence, constraint compliance, and the distinction between observed improvements and explanations of their underlying mechanisms. Applications in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support reveal three recurring requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and decisions that respect domain constraints. Building on this synthesis, we identify four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, diagnosis-guided repair, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

items.title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immune-related adverse events in a multi-phase validation study
items.abstract: Abstract Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. Here we show that agentic artificial intelligence coupled with human verification could enhance efficiency, performance and consistency for irAE assessment. We developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes. Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F 1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F 1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F 1 was 0.72–0.79. In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min ( P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

items.title: An AHP Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Software Vulnerability Assessment
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can assist software security review, but detecting more weaknesses may increase false alarms, unreliable patches, or higher costs. This methodological paper specifies a reproducible Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) framework for evaluating LLM-assisted vulnerability assessment in a synthetic banking-information application. Applying the framework to a local operational banking system was not feasible because obtaining the required security approvals was difficult; no production banking infrastructure was tested. Six objectives are linked to measurable indicators covering ground-truth completeness, detection, classification and severity assessment, secure remediation, reliability and resource use, and decision sensitivity. The protocol specifies 12 vulnerable and 12 corrected variants, four scenarios, repeated runs, blinded adjudication, CVSS v4.0 assessment, regression tests, and paired analysis. A comparison with SecurityEval, CyberSecEval, CyberSecEval 2, and BountyBench positions the proposed contribution as linking verified outcomes to stakeholder priorities rather than demonstrating superior benchmark performance. An exact reciprocal AHP example uses weights of 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, and 0.10. A separate simulation yields group weights of 0.3565, 0.2920, 0.2187, and 0.1328, with a consistency ratio of 0.0008. These are constructed examples, not elicited expert judgments. No LLM benchmarking was performed, and no model ranking is claimed. Empirical validation requires archived runs, independently assessed outcomes, and human stakeholder judgments; production transfer additionally requires institutional authorization and service-specific validation.

items.title: An Explainable AI Framework for Detecting Fraudulent Internship and Job Offers
items.abstract: Online portals have become commonplace for internships and job opportunities. With the increasing number of fraudulent internship and job offers, students find it difficult to differentiate between legitimate opportunities. Students face various risks such as fake recruiters, phishing, registration fee frauds, unrealistic offers, and other deceptions. This paper presents a study on an explainable artificial intelligence approach to detect fraudulent internship and job offers. It reviews existing artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and transformer based recruitment fraud detection algorithms and techniques and explainability methods such as SHAP and LIME for providing an interpretable explanation for a model’s outcome. It highlights the limitations of previous approaches such as using generic datasets and lacking internship-specific features, limited explainability and no user-centric explanations.

items.title: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Correlational Study of Students' Perceptions Following an AI-Supported Gamified Formative-Assessment Intervention
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined gamification attitudes, learning motivation, perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported speaking practice, and perceived Chinese language improvement among 71 university students in China's Greater Bay Area. It also explored perceived AI usefulness as a potential moderator. Gamification attitudes (r = .283, p = .017) and motivation (r = .49, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived improvement. Motivation remained a significant statistical predictor (β = .485, p < .001). Exploratory mediation analysis indicated an indirect association through motivation (effect = .080, bootstrap 95% Confidence Interval [.012, .189]). Drawing on these findings and theory, the study proposed a formative assessment workflow integrating AI-supported speaking practice and feedback, gamified practice, learner revision, and teacher guidance. The findings provided associational, not causal, evidence; the proposed workflow's effectiveness remains to be evaluated.

items.title: An Extended Adaptive Cuckoo Search Technique for Test Case Optimization
items.abstract: Model-driven test case production using Unified Modeling Language (UML) models has been widely explored to support early testing, often before system implementation. However, many existing techniques still struggle to produce optimal results efficiently, requiring a large number of iterations while achieving limited test coverage, as they rely on only a few UML models. To address these limitations, this study proposes an Extended Adaptive Cuckoo Search Technique (EACST), which builds and improves the Adaptive Cuckoo Search Algorithm (ACSA). Guided by the Design Science Research Methodology, the technique was conceptualized, developed, and evaluated through comparative experiments involving the Adaptive Cuckoo Search Algorithm (ACSA), the Enhanced Cuckoo Search Algorithm (ECSA), the hybrid Artificial Bee Colony and Simulated Annealing algorithm (ABC_SA), the Hybrid Graph-based Genetic Algorithm (HGGA), and the Differential Evolution algorithm with exponential crossover based on a learning strategy within the difference vector (DLS_DE). The initial evaluation was conducted using a single dataset to assess baseline performance under controlled conditions. The results demonstrate that EACST achieves optimal solutions using fewer iterations and reduced execution time compared to baseline techniques. Statistical validation using the Friedman and Wilcoxon tests further confirms these improvements, showing that EACST significantly outperforms ACSA, ECSA, ABC_SA, HGGA and DLS_DE. To ensure generalizability, a cross-system evaluation involving ten datasets was subsequently performed. The results show that EACST consistently generates a minimal test suite with maximum coverage, reduced effort, and fewer iterations compared to existing techniques. The proposed technique can be applied to a wide range of systems, including real-time environments such as Internet of Things systems and autonomous vehicles that utilize object-oriented paradigms. Future work will focus on developing hybrid approaches by integrating the proposed technique with Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning to further enhance performance.

items.title: An SSA-to-ADR Uncertainty Propagation Pipeline for Tether-Net Debris Capture Mission Planning
items.abstract: Tether-net capture and Space Situational Awareness (SSA) have developed as separate disciplines, and capture-dynamics studies almost universally prescribe a deterministic target state. This paper proposes an end-to-end SSA-to-ADR uncertainty propagation pipeline treating tether-net capture as a probabilistic decision problem conditioned on observational data quality. Three stages are coupled: characterisation of the debris state covariance from TLE and photometric light-curve data; propagation of that covariance to the ejection epoch through a state transition matrix and drag-driven process noise; and construction of a capture probability surface over the ejection parameter space. Applied to Telkom-3 (NORAD 38744) over eleven epochs, the framework shows that SSA data quality governs capture performance through the validity horizon of the predicted state, not through terminal navigation accuracy. The two branches differ by two to three orders of magnitude: the translational horizon is eight to nine hours (8.0–9.3 h), whereas the rotational horizon falls from 115 to 23 s across three analysis epochs as the spin period shortens from 20.3 to 11.8 s. Capture probability at a 30 s observation-to-ejection latency drops correspondingly from 0.90 to 0.36. Photometric support must therefore be obtained minutes, not hours, before ejection, and the ejection timed to within about a second of the predicted favourable rotational phase.

items.abstract: Ketidakpatuhan penggunaan Alat Pelindung Diri (APD) di area pemilahan sampah manual Tempat Pembuangan Akhir (TPA) memicu risiko kecelakaan kerja dan penyakit akibat kerja yang tinggi. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengkuantifikasi risiko serta mengidentifikasi akar masalah sistemik ketidakpatuhan APD massal (±50% pekerja) melalui pendekatan hibrida Root Cause Analysis (RCA) Level 4, Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS), dan Fuzzy Fault Tree Analysis (FFTA). Data faktual diaudit melalui triangulasi lima jenis data dan disaring menggunakan KNOT Chart, dengan jumlah responden 30 pekerja (50% dari populasi), dan 4 orang pakar dari bidang K3 dan operasional. Struktur kausalitas diklasifikasikan ke dalam empat tingkatan HFACS dan dikuantifikasi menggunakan Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFN) berbasis konsensus pakar. Hasil kuantifikasi menunjukkan nilai probabilitas terjadinya ketidakpatuhan massal (Top Event) sebesar P(TE) = 5,69%. Akar masalah paling kritis teridentifikasi pada level Organizational Influences (BE4: sistem pengadaan kaku tahunan tanpa buffer stock, FPV = 0.058) dan Unsafe Supervision (BE7: ketiadaan SOP Progressive Disciplinary System, FPV = 0.048). Berdasarkan temuan tersebut, dirumuskan matriks rekomendasi terintegrasi berbasis Hierarchy of Controls dan CAPA 4-Level untuk mentransformasi sistem pengawasan serta logistik K3 secara permanen dan berkelanjutan.

items.title: APLICAÇÕES DA INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA DETECÇÃO PRECOCE DA SEPSE PEDIÁTRICA: UMA REVISÃO SISTEMÁTICA
items.abstract: A sepse é uma das principais causas de morbimortalidade pediátrica em serviços de urgência. Seu diagnóstico precoce permanece desafiador devido à apresentação clínica inespecífica e à rápida evolução da doença. Nesse contexto, modelos de inteligência artificial (IA), especialmente baseados em machine learning e deep learning, têm sido propostos como ferramentas de apoio à decisão clínica para identificação precoce de pacientes em risco. Portanto, torna-se necessário avaliar o desempenho e a aplicabilidade de modelos de IA na detecção precoce da sepse pediátrica em cenários de urgência e emergência. Trata-se de uma revisão sistemática conduzida conforme as diretrizes PRISMA. A busca foi realizada no PubMed utilizando os descritores “artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “deep learning”, “pediatric sepsis” e “childhood sepsis”, abrangendo os últimos 10 anos. Foram incluídos estudos originais envolvendo pacientes de 0 a 18 anos com modelos de IA aplicados à sepse pediátrica. Dos 38 estudos identificados, 10 atenderam aos critérios de elegibilidade. Os estudos demonstraram desempenho consistente na predição precoce da sepse, com AUROC entre 0,80 e 0,92 e antecipação diagnóstica de 2 a 6 horas. Modelos que integraram variáveis clínicas e laboratoriais, especialmente XGBoost e redes neurais recorrentes, apresentaram maior acurácia. Estratégias baseadas exclusivamente em sinais vitais contínuos mostraram desempenho satisfatório, monitorização em tempo real e maior aplicabilidade em ambientes com recursos limitados. Apesar dos resultados promissores, persistem limitações relacionadas ao desenho retrospectivo, amostras reduzidas e heterogeneidade metodológica.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro: The good, the bad, the ugly
items.abstract: Apple Vision Pro (AVP), the headset Apple introduced as its first ``spatial computer,'' built by a single, vertically integrated vendor, entered the market in February 2024 and has since accumulated a fast-growing body of primary research spanning surgery, education, accessibility, design, and human-computer interaction. In this paper, we adopt the tripartite structure of Leone's 1966 film to organize a systematic review of this literature: we cataloged the validated, working applications of AVP (the good), the persistent technical and ergonomic limitations of a still-early-generation headset (the bad), and the ethical concerns and structural harms that follow from deliberate design, marketing, and deployment choices (the ugly). The review is built from a Scopus export of 218 records mentioning AVP, which we narrowed to 104 papers (2024--2026) with a primary focus on AVP, using explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria that we report in full, alongside a PRISMA-informed flow diagram of the screening process. We find the corpus heavily skewed toward validating benefits (medicine and surgery, education, and software tooling account for over half of the included papers) and comparatively thin on documented risks or misuse, a pattern we treat as a finding in its own right rather than a limitation to be explained away. We further show that several recurring issues, namely price, simulated social presence, and the gaze-tracking privacy architecture, resist a clean separation into ``bad'' or ``ugly'' using the published evidence alone, since both readings remain compatible with the same data. We close by identifying where the evidence base most needs to grow: independent risk and ethics research, bystander- and equity-focused study designs, and disclosure that would let researchers distinguish an engineering backlog from a structural choice.

items.title: Applications, ethics, and future agenda of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in tourism and hospitality: a systematic review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how tourism information is produced, exchanged, and consumed, yet its application scenarios, ethical consequences, and implications for service authenticity remain dispersed across a fast-growing literature. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this study identifies 3,825 records from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus and conducts a thematic synthesis of 461 publications, addressing three questions: where GenAI creates value on the supply and demand sides of tourism and hospitality, which ethical risks and organizational dilemmas accompany its adoption, and how machine intervention conflicts with interactional authenticity in service encounters. The synthesis indicates that GenAI operates as a double-edged sword. On the demand side, conversational and multimodal systems lower information search and decision-making costs; on the supply side, automated content generation unlocks operational capacity—yet these gains coexist with algorithmic bias and hallucination, privacy trade-offs, and employee deskilling. In service interactions, the computational essence of machine-generated empathy can elicit expectancy violations and algorithm aversion, weakening the interpersonal authenticity on which hospitality depends. The review integrates these findings into an efficacy-risk hedging framework embedded in a socio-technical account of human-AI collaboration and derives a tiered human-in-the-loop governance model. Its primary contribution is to link application-level benefits, systemic risks, and the authenticity conflict within one evidence-based framework, with each claim anchored in article-level evidence counts.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) proposals to counter AI cheating by students in non-invigilated assessment
items.abstract: Since ChatGPT3′s chatbot interface appeared in November 2022, AI cheating has re-incarnated a challenge for academia. It is accentuated in non-invigilated contexts during term as projects, essays and other documents are submitted (possibly) prior to proctored examinations. Cheating can be interpreted strategically as the institutional level, whereas its tactical expression examined in this article applies at the student-instructor interface. Here, we turn AI upon itself to see if it can address the dilemma it has created. A literature review regarding AI-facilitated cheating precedes a record of public and initial academic reactions. Having calibrated the problem, a method for addressing it is advanced. It enlists a set of AI large language models (LLMs) and search engines to rank six techniques by effectiveness in countering AI cheating. Analysis includes: descriptive assessment of model outputs; frequency counting, ranking and determination of unique and common techniques; and qualitative comparison of the suggestions tendered. The discussion relates the characteristics of the composite approaches to traditional assessment and evaluation. Ideas for ongoing research, and key recommendations form the conclusions.
