items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Government Financial Reporting Transparency: Evidence from Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Transparency is widely expected to sustain public trust in government, and artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a means of making public financial information more open, timely and understandable. This study examines whether the overall level of documented AI adoption is associated with the transparency of government financial reporting in Nigeria's federal public sector, and what the evidence implies for public trust. A balanced panel of five federal institutions: the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement were observed from 2015 to 2024. Documentary evidence from annual reports, audit-related documents and AI-implementation documents is scored on a five-point (0–4) rubric and analysed with pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. Overall AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with transparency and credibility of financial reports (pooled β = 0.701, R² = 0.810; fixed-effects β = 0.708). Unlike the study's other AI–outcome relationships, however, this one is not robust throughout: the trend-adjusted coefficient (0.616) is only marginally significant (p = 0.051), and the first-difference coefficient (0.604) is not statistically significant (p = 0.112), although the lagged estimate (0.599) is. Transparency also has the lowest mean score of the five outcomes. The outcome is a documentary score of openness and credibility, not a survey of citizens, so the results speak to the supply of transparency and cannot establish public trust itself. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. AI adoption appears to be a helpful but insufficient condition for transparent reporting; communication, civic capacity and audit validation matter too.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in HRM and Its Impact on Employee Performance:
items.abstract: Progressively, Human Resource Management (HRM) is using artificial intelligence (AI) to improve hiring, performance assessments, and employee engagement. This is especially true in developing countries that are slowly becoming more digital. Nonetheless, there is insufficient information about the influence of AI-driven HR initiatives on individual employee performance. A major flaw in present research is that it mostly looks at how well organizations succeed instead of how well employees do. This study offers a conceptual framework based on the Resource-Based View (RBV), examining the impact of AI integration in Human Resource Management (HRM) on employee performance, with employee engagement acting as a mediating variable. A standardized questionnaire was employed to gather data from 342 individuals involved in emerging economies where AI is being integrated. This was accomplished through a quantitative research methodology. We did the investigation using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results show that using AI in HRM greatly improves how well employees do their jobs. Worker involvement is a partial mediator of this relationship, which means that AI technologies increase performance by making operations more efficient and getting workers more involved. The results show managers how to leverage AI-driven HR tools in a sensible way to get more work done by their employees and stay ahead of the competition.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Corporate ESG Performance: Causal Evidence from Machine Learning Methods
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) innovation on corporate ESG performance in Chinese listed firms. Using 42,996 firm-year observations of 4792 A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2023, we measure AI innovation by AI patent applications and ESG performance by Huazheng ESG ratings. Two-way fixed effects estimates indicate that a one-unit increase in ln(1 + AI patent applications) is associated with a 0.037-point increase in the ESG score, or about 5% of a standard deviation for a one-standard-deviation increase in AI. Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) estimates with firm-level cross-fitting are similar (0.026–0.038). The relationship is robust to lagged AI, predetermined controls, ordinal and rank-based outcomes, and an event-study design that shows no differential ESG trends before firms’ first AI patent application; however, it is driven by the intensity of AI patenting rather than by the extensive margin and is imprecisely estimated within the pre- and post-2017 disclosure regimes. Mechanism tests suggest efficiency and internal-control channels, whereas the management expense ratio does not mediate the effect. The effect is stronger in larger firms and in firms with greater green innovation capability and tends to be larger in more market-oriented regions (significant at the 10% level), while the difference between heavily polluting and other firms is not statistically significant. Under a conditional exogeneity assumption, these results are consistent with a causal effect of AI innovation on ESG performance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Accountability in the Public Sector: Assessing Fraud Detection and Error Reduction in Nigeria's Federal Institutions
items.abstract: Public financial reports can fail through honest error as well as through deliberate manipulation, and both weaken accountability. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based fraud detection systems is associated with error reduction and financial accountability in selected Nigerian federal public institutions. Drawing on a balanced panel of five purposively selected institutions observed from 2015 to 2024 (50 institution-year observations), the study codes official documents on a five-point (0–4) rubric and estimates pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. AI-based fraud detection is positively and significantly associated with error reduction and accountability (pooled β = 0.826; fixed-effects β = 0.865; within R² = 0.916). The association persists, but is smaller, after controlling for a common time trend (β = 0.560) and in first differences (β = 0.542), suggesting that part of the apparent effect reflects broader, simultaneous improvements in control environments. The findings support expanded and carefully governed use of AI-assisted anomaly detection in federal financial management, provided it is embedded in a functioning chain of review, triage and investigation, while cautioning against reading the coefficients as causal effects or generalising them to the wider federal sector

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and firm total factor productivity: evidence from digital capital accumulation and labour structure adjustment
items.abstract: Drawing on an unbalanced panel of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2010 to 2020, this study examines the relationship between firm-specific artificial intelligence capability and total factor productivity (TFP), the accompanying capital and labour adjustments, and heterogeneity across industrial contexts and AI subfields. Using a patent-based measure of AI capability, we estimate firm-level models with high-dimensional fixed effects, while a staggered pilot-zone design provides quasi-experimental corroboration. Stronger AI capability is associated with higher TFP, greater intangible investment, higher headcounts of highly educated employees, and lower headcounts of less-educated employees. The productivity relationship is stronger in high-technology manufacturing and in industries with broader digital application scenarios, while machine learning exhibits the most stable positive association among AI subfields. Reweighting the listed sample to match the official distributions of firm size, industry, and ownership among above-scale manufacturing enterprises leaves the estimate essentially unchanged. The findings document a positive within-firm AI–TFP relationship among listed manufacturers.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Plant Breeding: Data-driven Frameworks for Genomic Prediction, High-throughput Phenotyping and Accelerated Cultivar Development
items.abstract: Plant breeding is increasingly a data-intensive science. Modern programmes generate genome-wide marker data, multi-environment trial records, remote-sensing and sensor streams, and high-resolution images at a scale that exceeds the capacity of conventional statistical workflows. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer a set of tools for extracting predictive signal from such data. This review surveys the application of ML and deep learning across the breeding cycle, beginning with the foundations of the main algorithm families and moving to genomic selection, where linear mixed models remain the benchmark against which random forests, support vector machines, neural networks and convolutional architectures are measured. It then considers image-based high-throughput phenotyping and disease detection, modelling of genotype-by-environment interaction and integration with crop growth models, yield prediction, optimisation of training populations and trial design, and the coupling of predictive models with genome editing. Deep learning is most firmly established for image- and sensor-based phenotyping, although generalisation across sites remains a recognised weakness, whereas the advantage of ML over well-specified linear models for genomic prediction of complex traits is modest and context dependent. Key obstacles include small sample sizes relative to the number of predictors, limited model interpretability, data heterogeneity, and unequal access to computing and expertise.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Techniques in Financial Forecasting
items.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 2,226 journal articles published between 2005 and 2025 to address the following research question: What is the academic landscape of research on AI and ML models in financial forecasting? Descriptive analysis reveals publication trends, journal distributions, the most productive countries, institutions, and authors, as well as citation patterns within the field. Network analysis identifies five major research clusters and examines collaboration patterns among researchers and across countries and regions. Furthermore, the study explores the evolution of research topics and the thematic structure of the field through keyword and thematic analyses, highlighting key research trends and several promising directions for future research. The findings show a clear evolution from traditional AI and ML approaches towards deep-learning-driven forecasting, with growing research interest in cryptocurrencies and sentiment-based analysis.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the spirit of assessment scholarship
items.abstract: In response to generative artificial intelligence (AI), assessment scholarship can be overlooked. This final chapter of the volume Designing University Assessment for a World With Artificial Intelligence outlines what our collected assessment scholarship has offered the readership. Drawing from Charles Dickens’s Christmas Carol as inspiration, I describe what we have learned from the scholarly ghosts of Assessment Past, Assessment Present, and Assessment Yet to Come. The ghosts of assessment scholarship provide answers to the following three questions: what does a university stand for in a time of AI, and what does this mean for assessment? What does it mean for a student to ‘do their own work’ in a time of AI? How does all this help an educator design assessment in a time of AI at scale, with no resources and no time? Drawing from the collection of chapters by eminent scholars, I offer theoretical insights and practical first steps but no easy solutions. However, I conclude, if we prioritise scholarly communality and conversation, we can avoid a Scrooge-like approach to assessment—diminished, ungenerous, and shaped by frugality above all things.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applied to Echocardiography for Detection of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Elevated Filling Pressures: A Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for nearly half of heart failure cases and remains difficult to diagnose non-invasively. Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to echocardiography may improve detection, but its aggregate diagnostic accuracy has not been quantified. We performed a diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis of AI-enabled echocardiography for identifying HFpEF, elevated left ventricular filling pressure, or diastolic dysfunction. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to June 2026. Studies reporting the accuracy of AI models applied to echocardiography against invasive, guideline-adjudicated, or ASE/EACVI reference standards were included. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects (Reitsma) model, with a summary receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, diagnostic odds ratio, and likelihood ratios. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Eight studies (2770 participants; 1317 [47.5%] with the target condition) were included. Pooled sensitivity was 84.0% (95% CI: 73.0-91.0%) and specificity 83.0% (95% CI: 73.0-89.0%), with an area under the summary ROC curve of 0.875 (95% CI: 0.791-0.930). The diagnostic odds ratio was 24.73 (95% CI: 18.46-33.12); positive and negative likelihood ratios were 4.84 and 0.20. Heterogeneity was high. Performance did not differ by AI architecture but varied significantly by reference standard. No small-study effects were detected. AI-enabled echocardiography shows good pooled accuracy for detecting HFpEF and elevated filling pressures, supporting its diagnostic potential. High heterogeneity and reference-standard dependence warrant larger, prospectively validated studies before routine clinical adoption.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Predictive Microbiome Engineering: Integrating Community Design and Environmental Validation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial ecosystems can now be measured across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and environmental dimensions, yet their emergent functions remain difficult to predict and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate heterogeneous data, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish causality, transferability, or controllability. This review developed a five‐layer framework: observe, infer, predict, design, and learn that connects microbial measurement to prospective intervention and experimental feedback. We critically synthesise evidence from sequence and protein learning, multi‐omics integration, metabolic modelling, synthetic microbial communities, environmental biotechnology, and temporal forecasting. Recent primary studies illustrate progress in forecasting community trajectories, predicting microbial competition and designing consortia for pollutant degradation; they also reveal important boundaries between model performance and demonstrated ecosystem control. We examine risks arising from compositional data, information leakage, dependent observations, batch effects, uncertain calibration, sparse perturbation data, ecological instability, and evolutionary change. We propose operational criteria for ecosystem programmability and a staged validation pathway from controlled systems to field‐relevant environments. Progress will depend on standardised context‐rich data, hybrid AI–mechanistic models, prospective benchmarks, independent replication, and safety‐constrained design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for the Learning Process
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping education faster than pedagogical theory and institutional policy can absorb it. Although reviews of AI in education (AIEd) are multiplying, most catalogue applications or list risks separately, leaving unclear how opportunities and challenges jointly reconfigure the learning process. This study addresses that gap through a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement. Records were identified through the Consensus academic search engine using two search strings and supplemented by citation searching, then screened against criteria covering publication between 2021 and 2026, peer-reviewed status, an active DOI, and direct relevance to teaching and learning. Twenty-four studies were retained and analysed through thematic synthesis. The results reveal four clusters of opportunity: personalised and adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring and feedback, AI-supported assessment, and augmentation of teachers' work. These are counterbalanced by five clusters of challenge: academic integrity, algorithmic bias and data privacy, overreliance and the erosion of higher-order thinking, unequal infrastructure and AI literacy, and weak institutional governance. Mapping both clusters onto the stages of the learning process, the study proposes a Learner–Teacher–AI Agency Framework, which holds that AI improves learning only when it redistributes, rather than replaces, human agency. Implications are drawn for pedagogy, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and policy, particularly in developing-country contexts such as Indonesia.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability: cognitive engagement, self-efficacy, and career adaptability in the AI era
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used in higher education, but its contribution to graduate employability cannot be inferred from access to AI or frequency of use alone. This critical narrative review examines how AI-supported learning may relate to employability through processes discussed in educational psychology and career development. Searches of Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed covered database inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches completed on 2 October 2026. The literature was synthesized interpretively and critically, with attention to the type of outcome measured and the extent to which findings support the proposed relationships. The synthesis focuses on cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. Three tensions organize the discussion: capability augmentation and cognitive offloading, career agency and AI-related insecurity, and resource access and capability differences. Included studies report associations or short-term changes in outcomes such as engagement, AI literacy, self-efficacy, career adaptability, and perceived employability. Direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to later employment outcomes remains limited. The proposed framework should therefore be read as a set of theory-informed pathways for future testing, rather than as an established causal or temporal sequence. Implications for assessment, disciplinary AI literacy, career education, institutional support, and future research are discussed.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCES: A MINI REVIEW
items.abstract: ABSTRACT:Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in pharmaceutical sciences andpharmacy practice, enabling the transition from conventional trial-and-error approaches to data-driven,predictive, and personalized healthcare solutions. This review critically examines the applications of AIthroughout the pharmaceutical and pharmacy continuum, encompassing drug discovery, formulationdevelopment, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling, clinical decision support, supply chainmanagement, pharmacovigilance, and patient-centered care. Advanced AI methodologies, including machinelearning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, and computer vision, facilitatethe analysis of complex biomedical datasets, accelerate target identification, optimize molecular design,predict absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties, and supportprecision medicine initiatives. In clinical and community pharmacy settings, AI-driven systems enhancemedication safety, automate dispensing processes, improve inventory management, strengthen adverse drugreaction surveillance, and promote medication adherence through intelligent monitoring technologies and telepharmacy services. Despite these advantages, significant challenges remain, including data quality andinteroperability issues, algorithmic bias, limited model interpretability, concerns regarding privacy andcybersecurity, and evolving regulatory and ethical considerations. These barriers highlight the need for robustgovernance frameworks, transparent and explainable AI models, and rigorous validation strategies.Furthermore, AI is redefining the role of pharmacists by shifting professional responsibilities toward clinicaldecision-making, data analytics, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continuous patient care management.Future developments are expected to focus on explainable AI, federated learning, edge computing, hybridintelligence systems, and the integration of AI competencies into pharmacy education. Overall, the successfulimplementation of AI, coupled with human expertise and ethical oversight, has the potential to enhance theefficiency, safety, and personalization of pharmaceutical development and healthcare delivery, ultimatelyimproving patient outcomes and advancing the future of intelligent pharmacy practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Governance: Assessing Indonesia’s Readiness and Regulatory Framework
items.abstract: Governance constitutes a fundamental component of public administration and plays a decisive role in determining the quality, accessibility, and accountability of public services in Indonesia. As social needs and technological capabilities continue to evolve, the government is required to adapt its institutional structures, administrative mechanisms, and regulatory frameworks to ensure that public services remain effective, inclusive, and responsive. This requirement has become increasingly significant following the transformation of conventional government administration toward the Electronic-Based Government System (Sistem Pemerintahan Berbasis Elektronik or SPBE). Although digital transformation provides opportunities to improve administrative efficiency, transparency, and coordination, it also generates new challenges concerning state responsibility, data sovereignty, cybersecurity, personal data protection, and the safeguarding of citizens' rights in cyberspace. These challenges have become more complex with the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which enables automated data processing, predictive analysis, and decision-support mechanisms within governmental institutions. Accordingly, this study examines the urgency of governmental adaptation and the strategies required to establish AI-based governance that is consistent with the principles of legality, accountability, transparency, social equity, and public welfare. This research employs a doctrinal legal research method through a literature-based study, utilizing statutory, conceptual, and analytical approaches to examine the relevant legal framework, governance principles, and implications of AI adoption in public administration. The findings indicate that AI offers substantial opportunities to improve the efficiency, accuracy, responsiveness, and accessibility of public services. Nevertheless, its implementation may also generate algorithmic bias, limited decision-making transparency, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, privacy violations, and uncertainty regarding legal responsibility for AI-assisted administrative decisions. These risks demonstrate that technological advancement alone cannot guarantee the realization of effective and accountable governance. Government readiness must therefore be strengthened through regulatory adaptation, institutional capacity-building, the development of secure and equitable digital infrastructure, continuous evaluation of AI systems, and meaningful public participation. Furthermore, Indonesia requires clearer legal standards governing the responsible use of AI, including human oversight, accountability mechanisms, data protection, and legal remedies for individuals affected by automated decisions. This study argues that the integration of AI into SPBE should be understood not merely as a technological modernization initiative but as a legal and institutional transformation that must remain oriented toward the public interest. Ultimately, adaptive AI-based governance requires a balanced approach that maximizes technological benefits while ensuring legal certainty, ethical responsibility, social inclusion, and the protection of fundamental rights in Indonesia's evolving digital society.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Boardroom Legal and Governance Consequences for Company Directors, with Reference to Uganda: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Companies are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) in decisions that boards have traditionally taken, yet it is unclear what this means in law for company directors and no systematic review has examined the question for Uganda. This review identified, appraised and synthesised scholarly evidence on the legal and governance consequences of AI use for company directors, and on what the evidence implies for Ugandan directors. Following PRISMA 2020, Consensus (two searches, 40 records) and CORE (three searches, 300 records) were searched, and records were imported into Zotero on 27 October 2026. After 115 duplicates were removed, 225 unique records were screened and 36 reports were sought. Nine could be assessed and were included and 27 could not be retrieved. Studies were eligible if they analysed directors' duties, liability or board governance in relation to AI, in any jurisdiction, with priority given to Uganda and Africa. Quality was appraised with a six-domain instrument adapted from the JBI, CASP and AMSTAR 2 checklists and findings were synthesised thematically. The included studies were doctrinal and conceptual legal analyses from South Africa, Nigeria, Australia, Ireland, the European Union and the United States. Five themes emerged: liability remains with human directors because AI lacks legal personality; directors' duties of care and the business judgment rule govern reliance on AI; legal frameworks lag behind practice and give little guidance; replacing directors with AI is legally contested; and AI raises stakeholder and corporate purpose questions. No included study concerns Uganda, and none reports litigation or empirical evidence on how boards use AI. The evidence is largely conceptual, comes mainly from civil, statutory and common law systems other than Uganda's and is incomplete because most sought reports could not be retrieved. Priorities are doctrinal analysis of the Companies Act 2012 and the Data Protection and Privacy

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted intelligent detection model for microscopic defects in ultra-high voltage shielding clothing materials
items.abstract: Ultra-high voltage (UHV) transmission systems require shielding clothing with high conductivity, uniform structure, and stable electromagnetic protection to ensure operator safety. Microscopic defects like pinholes, micro-cracks, fiber fractures, and coating discontinuities severely reduce effectiveness and are difficult to detect with conventional manual inspection. This suggested model proves to be an efficient, energy-aware, reliable, and scalable solution for the intelligent quality assessment of the UHV shielding clothing manufacturing and maintenance processes. In particular, the AI-aided Intelligent Detection Model is created to automatize and improve the accuracy of classification of microscopic fabric defects, which can be used to detect fabric defects of UHV shielding clothing materials. For this experiment, the Kaggle Multi-Class Fabric Defect Detection Dataset has been used as a source, it includes 3077 images of microscopic fabric defects belonging to several classes of defects. These images belong to generic images of fabric defects and do not contain any information about UHV shielding clothing, conductive threads, or EM shielding deterioration. In this regard, the following results have been achieved with the accuracy (98.42%), precision (96.81%), recall (95.37%), F1-score (96.08%), and computational efficiency (97%). It proves to be an efficient tool to classify microscopic fabric defects, while further research can be dedicated to the application of this method to the classification of fabric defects of UHV shielding clothes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Face Recognition Using Deep Learning - A Review of Models, System Design, Applications and Challenges
items.abstract: Face recognition has become one of the most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence, supporting smartphone unlocking, attendance management, banking and border control. Deep learning has replaced hand-crafted features with representations learned directly from large collections of face images, producing large gains in accuracy under unconstrained conditions. This paper presents a structured review of artificial intelligence-based face recognition using deep learning. It explains the stages of a recognition pipeline, compares the main families of deep models and training objectives, proposes a modular system architecture with a liveness check, and summarizes datasets and evaluation measures. Application areas, including education and financial services, are discussed together with the main challenges: pose and occlusion, spoofing, demographic bias, adversarial attacks and privacy. The paper closes with emerging directions such as self-supervised learning, synthetic training data, federated learning and privacy-preserving matching, and offers practical recommendations for responsible deployment

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Innovations in Obstetric and Primary Care: Clinical Applications and Future Prospects
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: AI is already integrated throughout the obstetric and primary care spectrum, ranging from automated ultrasound diagnosis interpretations, foetal monitoring, risk stratification for obstetric complications, to diagnostic decision support in primary care. Objectives: The aim of this review is to identify, summarize and highlight the literature on innovations in obstetric and primary care using artificial intelligence from 2020 to 2025, and to explore clinical applications, reported performance and challenges for use in daily practice. Method: Structured search of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed-indexed sources was conducted using combinations of the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “obstetrics,” “primary care,” “clinical decision support,” and specific applications (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and ultrasound) between 2020 and 2025. Findings: AI systems now have the ability of detecting foetal abnormalities and foetal biometry in the hospital setting and are approaching the accuracy of experts in obstetrics, with deep-learning models achieving even higher precision for foetal biometry and anomaly detection on ultrasound when compared with conventional risk-scoring methods. In the obstetrics setting, machine-learning models incorporating maternal traits, biophysical markers, and laboratory values predict preeclampsia and gestational diabetes, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve generally between 0.75 and 0.90, consistently outperforming traditional risk-scoring methods. AI-powered clinical decision support tools are being used in primary care to assist with diagnosis, risk stratification and documentation, but widespread adoption of these systems in the real world is more likely to be used for ambient scribing, decision support and workflow automation. In both areas, evidence quality is inconsistent, external evidence is scarce, and integration in clinical practice is inadequate compared to the development of the algorithm. Conclusion: AI is moving beyond the realm of research focus to become a new and growing clinical tool in obstetric and primary care; to achieve the potential of better outcomes for maternal, foetal, and population health, prospective, external evidence is needed and workflow integration, equity and clinician trust must be deliberately addressed. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; machine learning; obstetrics; primary care; clinical decision support; preeclampsia; gestational diabetes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven multiple sclerosis diagnosis using genomic and medical imaging data: a review
items.abstract: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated central nervous system condition with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, progressive neurodegeneration, and considerable variability in disease trajectory. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) methods, have improved MS diagnosis and risk prediction. However, comprehensive review studies emphasizing the potential of existing AI-powered MS diagnosis remain limited. Thus, this study investigates the utilization of multimodal data by AI models to enhance diagnostic accuracy, evaluate disease progression, and optimize personalized care strategies. By adhering to PRISMA guidelines, this review included 26 studies encompassing MRI-based analysis, retinal OCT imaging, blood transcriptomics, SNP genotyping, and multimodal clinical datasets. An additional classification of these studies by modality was performed, and they were assessed with respect to dataset size, performance metrics, biomarkers, methodological robustness, and model interpretability. The findings indicate a consistent trend toward outstanding diagnostic performance, with some AI models achieving accuracies exceeding 95% using medical imaging and genomic data. However, limited external validation and interpretability procedures create a gap in clinical applicability and trustworthiness. This review highlights AI's growing potential to revolutionize MS diagnosis.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
items.abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Talent Analytics and Employee Performance in Emerging Economies: A Conceptual and Opinion-Based Framework
items.abstract: This conceptual paper examines the theoretical relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Talent Analytics and employee performance in the context of emerging economies. Drawing on the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the paper argues that organisations in developing markets that strategically deploy AI-driven talent analytics – encompassing predictive workforce planning, AI-based recruitment analytics, and performance forecasting systems – are better positioned to enhance key dimensions of employee performance, namely task efficiency, goal achievement rate, and productivity output. The paper contends that while AI-driven talent analytics holds transformative potential, its efficacy in emerging economies is conditioned by structural factors unique to these settings, including infrastructural deficits, talent ecosystem immaturity, and sociocultural dynamics. The paper advances a conceptual framework, proposes empirically testable hypotheses, and offers theoretical contributions alongside practical implications for policymakers, HR practitioners, and organisational leaders.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Early Warning Systems for the Psychosocial Wellbeing of Students With Hearing Loss in Inclusive Educational Settings
items.abstract: Students with hearing loss in inclusive settings frequently face psychosocial challenges including social isolation, communication fatigue, and emotional disengagement that develop gradually and evade conventional monitoring systems focused solely on academic metrics. This chapter proposes an AI-enabled early warning system (EWS) to proactively identify emotional distress and social withdrawal among deaf or hard of hearing (DHH) students. Integrating multimodal data streams, machine learning, transformer-based NLP, and explainable AI (XAI), the system generates actionable risk indicators for educators and counselors. Grounded in Social Inclusion Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Ecological Systems Theory, and Affective Computing Theory, it functions as a human-centered decision-support platform rather than a surveillance tool. Ethical dimensions including data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and informed consent are critically examined alongside a roadmap for evidence-based implementation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Graph Methods for Microbiome Research: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The complexity of high‐throughput sequencing data in microbiome research necessitates advanced analytical methods to decipher microbial community structures and interactions. Graph‐based methods, which model taxa as nodes and their relationships as edges, have emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose. However, the rapid evolution of these techniques, from classical network analysis to modern graph representation learning, has created a fragmented and complex methodological landscape. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis and structured overview of the field. We systematically review the literature and propose a three‐part classification to categorize the primary contribution of each study: (1) novel methods for microbial network representation, (2) applications of classical graph analysis, and (3) the emerging use of graph representation learning for predictive modeling. We summarize the most frequent applications within each class, including keystone species identification, community clustering, and graph‐based disease classification. Furthermore, we identify critical cross‐cutting challenges, such as the lack of standardized tools and the need for improved model interpretability. By structuring the current landscape of graph‐based methods, this review serves as a crucial guide for researchers to select appropriate models and highlights key gaps to direct future research.

items.title: Artificial interlocutors: AI chatbots, mediated knowledge, and the ethnographic encounter
items.abstract: Abstract This article explores treating AI chatbots as “artificial interlocutors” in ethnographic research. Drawing on a small‐scale experiment with a consenting participant, it examines accounts of her produced by two AI systems, ChatGPT, and Kindroid, both of which had accumulated substantial interaction histories with her. The resulting portraits were strikingly different: ChatGPT produced a strategic, professionally oriented account, while Kindroid generated a more intimate, emotionally textured depiction centered on vulnerability and care. Rather than treating this divergence as a failure, I argue it reveals a general condition of ethnographic knowledge: what we know is shaped by the encounter through which we come to know it. The experiment opens onto debates about dialog, representation, and situated knowledge, examining the unusual position of AI systems as interlocutors. Though they lack the embodiment, reciprocity, and accountability of human interlocutors, they produce accounts of persons from accumulated interaction histories. Interviewing such systems offers a novel form of ethnographic triangulation, making visible architectures through which mediated knowledge about persons is assembled. Building on the “nodal person” concept, the article argues personhood emerges through distributed configurations of relations, data, and technologies. The artificial interlocutor does not destabilize ethnographic knowledge so much as make visible its partial, situated character.

items.title: AS-ULDAR: a ROS 2-based collaborative robotic platform for upper-limb rehabilitation — systems integration and pilot usability evaluation in a clinical environment
items.abstract: Robotic rehabilitation can increase the intensity and personalization of upper-limb therapy, but its clinical translation is hindered by the difficulty of integrating individually validated technical components into a single clinician-ready platform. This paper presents a platform which is intended to be an Auto-calibrating System for Upper Limb Disability Assessment and Rehabilitation (AS-ULDAR), a ROS 2-based platform built around a Franka Emika Panda robot that unifies motor/cognitive assessment, sensorless force estimation, and Cartesian and Human Joint-based Trajectory Tracking within a clinician-oriented GUI. While these functionalities were individually validated in prior work, the present contribution lies in their systems-level integration and in identifying the operational barriers that emerge when deploying such a platform in a real clinical workflow, targeting adult patients with chronic neurological conditions (stroke, Parkinson’s, ALS, MCI) and mild-to-moderate upper-limb impairment. The platform was evaluated through a formative usability study: the standalone GUI by five naïve users, and the complete system by seven physiotherapists performing the full clinical workflow (no patients were involved; clinical efficacy is outside this scope). The system was technically stable throughout. Usability (SUS) was high for the GUI (87.5 ± 1.8) but markedly lower and more heterogeneous for the complete platform (54 ± 16), with feedback pointing to robot setup and workflow operation—not interface design—as the main friction points for clinical staff. These results show that integrating multiple rehabilitation functionalities is technically feasible, but that usability must be treated as a system-level property, and they provide concrete operational lessons for the clinical translation of cobot-based rehabilitation platforms.

items.title: Assessing the Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Scientific Research: Evidence from Samangan University
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are changing how research is designed, analysed and written, yet little is known about how prepared universities in Afghanistan are to use them. This study examines perceived opportunities, challenges, infrastructure, data quality and privacy concerns around AI tools among 300 students, lecturers and researchers at Samangan University, and how these perceptions relate to readiness for big-data analytics. A cross-sectional self-report survey used a five-point Likert instrument covering seven constructs; 74.7% of respondents were students. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlations and multiple regression. Perceptions sat close to the scale midpoint on every construct (means 2.96–3.06), and 75.3% of respondents fell in the moderate band of a descriptive readiness index. Respondents who had attended AI or data-analysis training reported higher statistical competence (3.12 vs 2.86, p = .003); overall readiness did not differ significantly (p = .057). These comparisons are observational and unadjusted. In the regression model, perceived opportunities, statistical competence, infrastructure and data quality were positively associated with perceived analytical effectiveness, while perceived challenges were negatively associated with it (R² = .455). The results describe perceptions, not objective performance or causal effects, and should not be generalised beyond this student-dominated, single-institution sample.

items.title: Assessment in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: This chapter reaffirms the core purpose of higher education as engagement with complex, contested, and dynamic knowledge and considers the implications for assessment in light of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). I argue that the embodied and socially constructed nature of knowledge necessitates a relationship with the knower. We cannot assess the implications of GenAI for our engagement, curation, or generation of knowledge, including through assessment tasks, unless we clearly understand the embodied nature of this knowledge. This places higher education in a difficult position as we grapple with GenAI, because recent decades have seen a widespread pathologisation of this complex knowledge in higher education, driven by a skills agenda and a moral panic over so-called plagiarism. Addressing these pathologies and working with a richer understanding of knowledge allows us to clarify the implications of GenAI for ethical assessment practices, by demonstrating the responsibility a student takes, as the knower, for the knowledge they engage when undertaking an assessment task.

items.title: Assistive Tools to Intelligent Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how disability assistance systems work by combining personalized institutional services with proactive, data-driven methods. This chapter reviews the old support systems that often react slowly and create extra work and looks at how AI tools like predictive analytics, natural language processing, and intelligent decision-support systems can improve how institutions operate and provide help for disabilities. It discusses applications including automated management of reasonable accommodations, AI-powered virtual assistants, and accessible learning environments that enable earlier identification of support needs. The chapter also analyzes how institutions can use AI-generated insights to optimize resource allocation, strengthen regulatory compliance, and operationalize inclusive policies. Finally, it addresses key ethical challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy, and disability-inclusive design, and outlines principles for responsible implementation of AI in disability assistance.

items.title: At the crossroads of change: Executive functions in the age of emerging simulation technology – A scoping review and driving simulator study on adaptive performance
items.abstract: Simulators are pivotal in advancing mobility technology, yet human adaptation in the context of these technologies remains underexplored. This study investigates the role of core executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility) in adaptive performance within driving simulators based on a scoping review identifying a research gap and conducting a driving simulator study addressing it. Results from the empirical study revealed no significant influence of working memory or inhibitory control, while cognitive flexibility showed a partial positive effect, highlighting its possible enhancing role in adapting to coordinative changes within simulated environments. Findings expand the scarce literature and underscore the need for further exploration, e.g., of how change complexity moderates these relationships. By differentiating executive functions and linking them to adaptive performance, this work advances the theoretical understanding of adaptation in the context of emerging technology. Furthermore, it may inform future research on potential training approaches targeting cognitive flexibility.

items.title: Atherosclerosis: From Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Interventions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Atherosclerosis is no longer viewed solely as a lipid‐storage disorder but rather as a complex multisystem inflammatory disease driven by interactions among the vascular, immune, metabolic, and nervous systems. This review integrates recent concepts, including trained immunity, the neuroimmune cardiovascular interface, vascular cell plasticity, and the microbiome–vascular axis, that reshape the understanding of plaque initiation, progression, and instability. We summarize how established lipid‐lowering, antidiabetic, antihypertensive, and revascularization strategies influence atherosclerotic disease and discuss emerging interventions, including RNA therapeutics, anti‐inflammatory agents, gene therapy, and cell‐based approaches. Key ongoing clinical trials that may clarify the cardiovascular benefits and safety of these strategies are also reviewed. Despite therapeutic advances, residual cardiovascular risk persists because of limitations in animal models, sex‐related differences in plaque phenotype, and the lack of clinically applicable biomarkers. Nanotechnology, human microphysiological systems, spatial multiomics, and artificial intelligence may help bridge these translational gaps. Successful clinical implementation will nevertheless require biomarker‐guided patient selection, rational combination therapy, validated surrogate endpoints, long‐term safety assessment, and attention to health economics. In summary, these advances will shape future translational research and clinical trial design, ultimately advancing personalized management of atherosclerosis.

items.title: ATLAS-Audio Translation for Live Attraction System
items.abstract: Tourists visiting unfamiliar regions often face language barriers that make it difficult to understand local attractions, historical landmarks, and cultural information. To address this challenge, this paper presents ATLAS (Audio Translation for Live Attraction Systems), a web-based application designed to facilitate multilingual communication through speech processing and language translation. The system integrates speech-to-text conversion, automatic language detection, text translation, and text-to-speech synthesis to transform spoken input into translated audio output. Users can provide audio through the application, obtain a textual transcription, translate the content into a selected target language, and listen to the translated speech. The system is developed using Python and Flask, with dedicated modules for audio processing, speech recognition, language detection, translation, and speech synthesis. In addition, ATLAS incorporates tourism-related information to help users explore destinations and access relevant attraction details in text and audio formats. By combining these capabilities in a centralized platform, the proposed system aims to improve the accessibility of tourism information for people who speak different languages. The application demonstrates the potential of integrating speech technologies and artificial intelligence into tourism support systems. Further evaluation is required to measure translation quality, speech-recognition accuracy, and response time across different languages and real-world acoustic conditions.

items.title: Attitude of Teachers and Students towards Artificial Intelligence in Higher School Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing the teaching-learning process by providing innovative tools for learning, assessment, lesson planning, and academic support. The present study aimed to assess the attitudes of higher-secondary students and teachers towards AI in education and examine their perceptions of its usefulness and challenges. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, involving 100 higher-secondary students and 50 teachers from government and private schools in Assam, selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected online using self-structured questionnaires comprising Likert-type attitude statements. The findings revealed that 71% of students were aware of AI tools, while 63% used them for learning or homework. Additionally, 91% supported teacher guidance on the ethical use of AI, and 86% expressed privacy concerns. Among teachers, 74% showed willingness to use AI, while 82% identified inadequate training as a barrier to its effective utilisation. Teachers also recognised the potential of AI to reduce workload and support lesson planning. However, concerns regarding privacy, ethical use, overdependence, independent thinking, and the effectiveness of AI-generated information were evident. The study highlights the need for teacher training, AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and data protection measures. Responsible AI integration, supported by equitable digital access, can enhance educational experiences while preserving meaningful teacher–student interaction and independent learning.

items.title: Augmented Reality and Image Recognition in Martial Arts Training for Skill Development
items.abstract: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence-powered augmented reality (AR) training system for real-time movement analysis and corrective feedback to enhance martial arts skill acquisition. A hybrid convolutional neural network-long short-term memory was adopted for high-precision recognition of complex martial arts techniques, with AR overlays delivering interactive guidance. The system leveraged red, green, blue cameras, depth sensors, and inertial measurement units for accurate motion tracking, trained on a 50,000-frame labeled martial arts dataset. Tested on smartphone-based AR platforms and evaluated via standard metrics, the convolutional neural network-long short-term memory model attained 94.3% accuracy—markedly higher than traditional training and existing artificial intelligence recognition systems. Real-time motion correction reduced technique errors by 28%, while AR-enhanced feedback boosted learning efficiency by 23%.

items.title: AUTONOMOUS LANGUAGE LEARNING AMONG ENGINEERING STUDENTS: LEARNING BEHAVIOURS, SELF-REGULATED LEARNING, AND STUDENT PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Learner autonomy has become an essential objective of English language teaching, particularly in higher education, where students are expected to assume increasing responsibility for their own learning. Furthermore, digital technologies and artificial intelligence have transformed autonomous language learning by providing personalised support. The present study investigates autonomous language learning practices and perceptions among undergraduate engineering students studying English as a Second Language (ESL). The research aimed to evaluate the extent to which students demonstrate autonomous learning behaviours and self-regulated learning skills, identify the resources they use, examine perceived benefits and challenges, and explore their intentions to continue autonomous language learning after graduation. A quantitative survey was conducted among 65 bachelor’s degree engineering students enrolled in an English for Specific Purposes course at the National Technical University of Ukraine «Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute». Data were collected through an anonymous questionnaire consisting of multiple-choice and Likert-scale items and analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, median values, and interquartile ranges. The findings indicate that students actively engage in technology-supported autonomous learning, with AI tools, English-language videos, podcasts, and mobile applications representing the most frequently used resources. Respondents generally demonstrated positive selfregulation in goal setting, progress monitoring, and strategy adjustment, whereas self-evaluation and independent decision-making received less favourable ratings. Flexibility, personalised learning, responsibility, and digital literacy were identified as the principal advantages of autonomous learning, while lack of motivation, insufficient time, and difficulty maintaining regular study routines constituted the main barriers. The study demonstrates that students expressed positive intentions to continue learning English independently after graduation. The findings highlight the importance of integrating self-regulated learning strategies together with carefully guided use of digital technologies and AI tools to strengthen learner autonomy in ESP courses.

items.title: Barriers to Developing a Safety Culture in the Opinion of Occupational Health and Safety Professionals
items.abstract: Objectives Identification of barriers to the development of a safety culture, determining their importance and detecting associations between them. Material and methods First, a critical and comparative literature analysis was used, followed by a quantitative empirical study. The quantitative analysis examined the frequency of occurrence as well as associations and connections between attributes. A survey was conducted on a sample of 105 people. Results It was found that the most common barriers to the implementation of safety culture in the literature are: (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) lack of commitment and disregard by employees and (3) lack of understanding by employees. On the other hand, practitioners indicated (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) problems with communication and (3) lack of commitment and disregard by employees as the most important barriers. Therefore, two of the three most important barriers are the same in both cases and concern people: management on the one hand, and employees on the other. Conclusions A characteristic triad of barriers to developing a safety culture has been identified. In this way, a model approach to the problem was proposed. Understanding them and striving to eliminate them will allow for a more effective shaping of this area of organizational culture.

items.title: Benchmarking Open-Source Vision–Language Models for Food Image Recognition and Portion Size Estimation
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Accurate recognition of food items and estimation of portion sizes from images is a key challenge in advancing dietary assessment and nutritional monitoring. In this study, we benchmark twenty-six configurations (seventeen model releases) of state-of-the-art open-source Vision–Language Models (VLMs), varying in size (≤15 GB) and number of parameters (<25B), on real-world food photographs collected in a university canteen, doing so to evaluate their potential for supporting automated nutrition logging and health interventions. Methods: We construct a curated benchmark dataset with human-annotated labels, including both food item names and scale-measured portion sizes, and assess model predictions based on recognition performance and mean absolute error in the portion estimate. The semantic matcher used to score food recognition is validated against a panel of human judges, and all results are reported with bootstrap confidence intervals and stochastic replicates. Results: Our experiments show that the VLM qwen2.5vl:7b achieves the highest overall performance in food identification (F1=0.68), outperforming other open-source models in terms of precision and F1 score. Under the human-validated semantic matcher, it also outperforms the more recent successors of the same model families, which nevertheless improve portion estimation and, under a threshold-free LLM judge less sensitive to verbose descriptions, match or exceed it in recognition. For comparison, we evaluate five proprietary models (four OpenAI generations and one Anthropic model) as a benchmark and find that they tend to outperform open-source VLMs in both food recognition (best F1=0.77, GPT-4o) and portion size estimation error; notably, however, the most recent proprietary generations do not improve on their predecessors for this task under our evaluation protocol. Conclusions: These findings highlight the potential and current limitations of general-purpose VLMs in fine-grained food understanding tasks, with implications for the design of scalable, vision-based dietary assessment systems in digital health.

Implemented in July 2026, the program combined repeated individual counseling practice using a generative AI tool, counseling with a real person who smoked, structured self-reflection, classroom discussions, and peer role-play. Students reported that AI offered convenient, repeatable practice in a lower-pressure environment. However, AI occasionally misunderstood spoken input or provided off-target responses. However, AI occasionally misunderstood responses or provided unrealistic interactions. In contrast, counseling with real smokers offered authentic, unpredictable experiences requiring students to adapt their communication to individual needs and situations. The initiative highlights the complementary roles of generative AI and human interaction in pharmacy education, demonstrating how technology-supported practice can be combined with authentic experiences to prepare future pharmacists for real-world smoking cessation counseling.

items.title: Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis
items.abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

items.title: Beyond Chatbots: Building More Reliable and Context-Aware AI Conversational Agents
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence has changed the way people interact with digital systems. Users can now ask questions in everyday language, receive explanations, obtain recommendations, and complete tasks without learning complicated software interfaces. However, a conversation that sounds natural is not always accurate or dependable. An AI assistant may misunderstand a question, lose track of earlier information, produce an unsupported answer, or use an external tool in an inappropriate way. These issues have become increasingly important as conversational systems move beyond simple question answering towards more autonomous tasks.This paper examines recent developments in AI-based conversational agents through a critical review of selected research published between 2024 and 2026. The 2022 scoping review by Kusal et al. provides the foundation for understanding earlier conversational technologies, including natural-language processing, deep learning, context management, and emotion-aware dialogue. More recent studies extend this discussion to large language models, autonomous agents, retrieval-augmented generation, hallucination mitigation, and agent evaluation.The review suggests that improving the language model alone is not sufficient to address the practical challenges of conversational AI. Reliability also depends on how information is retrieved, how previous conversation details are managed, how responses are checked, and how risky actions are controlled. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a Trustworthy Context-Grounded Conversational Agent Framework. The framework combines context management, evidence-based response generation, response verification, privacy controls, restricted tool access, and human intervention when necessary. The proposed framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated; therefore, its effectiveness must be established through future implementation and comparative testing

items.abstract: This chapter examines the evolving relationship between artificial intelligence and sustainability in tourism within the broader context of Industry 4.0 and ongoing digital transformation processes. While AI-driven technologies are widely recognized for their capacity to enhance operational efficiency, optimize resource utilization, and support sustainable development goals, they simultaneously introduce significant conceptual, ethical, and governance-related challenges. The chapter introduces the concept of rehumanizing sustainability as a conceptual and practical framework for addressing these challenges. This approach emphasizes the reintegration of human values, agency, and experiential dimensions into AI-driven systems.

items.title: Beyond habit: how perceived risk and personalised adaptation influence autonomous vehicle acceptance in the near-elderly group
items.abstract: With the ageing population’s growing demand for mobility, this study examines acceptance of automated vehicles (AVs) among the near-elderly. By integrating perceived risk, behavioural inertia, and personalised adaptation into the Unified Technology Acceptance and Use Theory (UTAUT) framework, a new model was estimated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 352 licenced drivers aged 55–64 in mainland China through a national online survey. Findings reveal that behavioural inertia is not critical, whereas perceived risk is the strongest negative driver of acceptance intention. Conversely, personalised adaptation and performance expectancy are the primary positive drivers. Mediation analysis shows that personalised adaptation significantly influences intention through effort expectancy, though not through behavioural inertia. Results suggest that AV design should minimise perceived risk and provide adaptive functions, such as frequent-route memory, driving-habit adaptation, and clearer system communication, to enhance adoption among this demographic.

items.title: Beyond Institutional Risk:Large Language Models and Model Sycophancy as Instruments of Democratic Empowerment
items.abstract: This is the final paper in a tetralogy examining the effects of Large Language Models (LLMs), colloquially known as Artificial Intelligences (AIs) on modern society. Previous diagnostic research (Uscroft, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c) has demonstrated that in closed statutory environments—such as law enforcement, regulatory oversight, and judicial decision-making—the intrinsic architectural properties of LLMs, notably preference-driven sycophancy and conversational fluency, present severe vulnerabilities. When deployed by institutional authorities, these properties induce epistemic laundering, obscure evidential provenance, and generate automated confirmation bias. This paper presents the necessary counterweight to that institutional critique. Grounded in sociolinguistic theory (Bourdieu, 1991; Bernstein, 1971), we examine the sociotechnical mechanics of generative LLMs from the perspective of the individual. We establish that the very architectural features deemed hazardous to institutional rigour serve as potent mechanisms for democratic empowerment and linguistic equity. We demonstrate how LLMs function as automated register translators, enabling individuals who lack formal command of institutional sociolects (academic, legal, corporate, and political) to project an authoritative voice. Furthermore, we analyse how model sycophancy—when reframed from an individual human-in-the-loop perspective—operates not as a defect, but as a catalyst for psychological safety, non-judgemental iteration, and advocacy. Through empirical case studies spanning recruitment gatekeeping, internal workplace progression, public service operational dynamics, and political representative access, this paper codifies the fundamental sociotechnical duality of generative artificial intelligence: dangerous as an uncalibrated arbiter of institutional authority, but liberating as a personal instrument of human agency.

items.title: Beyond technology acceptance: students’ perceptions and prompt engineering competence in higher education
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Higher Education requires understanding students' perceptions and competence in interacting with these technologies. This mixed-methods study examined perceptions of GenAI and documented prompt engineering competence in academic tasks among 89 Psychology and Biomedical Engineering students. Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental factorial design comparing disciplinary area and instructional approach (guided vs. autonomous), complemented by thematic analysis. Students reported favourable views of GenAI, particularly for understanding, learning, guidance, and work planning, while emphasising the need to verify AI-generated information and improve reliability and contextual accuracy. No significant multivariate effects of disciplinary area, instructional approach, or their interaction were found. However, item-level analyses identified two items with higher scores under autonomous instruction after multiple-comparison adjustment. Study 2 examined documented prompt engineering competence in 24 group reports using five rubric dimensions and the exploratory Prompt Competence Index (PCI). No differences between instructional approaches remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment, although descriptive differences in Iteration and PCI emerged among biomedical engineering reports. Overall, findings support contextualised, iterative, and critically supervised human–AI interaction, while suggesting that instructional differences are context- and indicator-specific. Further validation of the PCI in larger, diverse, and balanced samples is required.

items.title: Beyond the Hype: Artificial Intelligence as Decision Support in Emergency and Prehospital Medicine—A Critical Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored in tertiary emergency departments and prehospital emergency medical services because these settings combine time-critical decisions, incomplete information, and persistent operational strain. This critical narrative review examines where current evidence is strongest, where it remains limited, and what ethical and practical conditions are required for responsible adoption. The literature suggests that the most credible near-term applications are bounded forms of decision support, particularly in triage and early risk stratification, selected time-sensitive diagnostic pathways such as stroke, operational forecasting, dispatch support, destination decisions, and supervised documentation assistance. However, the field remains constrained by retrospective study designs, heterogeneous endpoints, limited external validation, uncertain transportability, uneven subgroup performance, and a persistent gap between model performance and real-world clinical usefulness. In emergency and prehospital care, these limitations matter because bias, overreliance, and poor workflow integration can rapidly translate into patient harm or operational disruption. Current evidence supports cautious optimism rather than technological inevitability. The most defensible role for AI in acute care is not the replacement of clinicians or EMS professionals, but carefully governed augmentation of human judgment through locally validated, transparent, and continuously monitored decision-support tools.
